entry.title: Sony RIALTO 65 Announced – 65mm Camera Extension for VENICE 2, 9.6K Open Gate, 16-bit X-OCN
entry.summary: Sony’s RIALTO 65 is now official, and it puts a 65mm format sensor into a compact head that connects to an existing VENICE 2 body, on a cable or attached directly. It reads out 9.6K Open Gate, records 16-bit X-OCN internally, and arrives in the first half of 2027. I am at Sony’s
entry.content:
Sony’s RIALTO 65 is now official, and it puts a 65mm format sensor into a compact head that connects to an existing VENICE 2 body, on a cable or attached directly. It reads out 9.6K Open Gate, records 16-bit X-OCN internally, and arrives in the first half of 2027. I am at Sony’s event at Pinewood Studios today, where Sony is showing us the system.

When Sony announced the RIALTO 65 as a development project in June, we covered it with a long list of open questions about resolution, recording, and lens mounts. Today Sony answers most of them. The RIALTO 65 (model CBK-6510XS) uses a 53.75 x 35.83mm sensor with a 1.5:1 aspect ratio, about 2.2 times the area of full frame. According to Sony, it is among the largest sensors in any commercially available cinema camera. The head weighs about 1.5kg / 3.3lb, and it offers dual base ISO 2500 and 10000, with 15+ stops of latitude at ISO 2500.

This article is based on Sony’s press material. I will see the system at Pinewood today, and we will publish an interview video from the event in the next few days. So, for my own impressions, stay tuned.

A taller 65mm sensor

For me, the most interesting part is not the size but the shape. ARRI’s ALEXA 65 and the newer ALEXA 265 have had the digital 65mm market almost to themselves for years. Their sensor has a similar width, but a much wider aspect ratio of close to 2.1:1. Sony goes taller, to 1.5:1, which gives the proportions of a still photography frame.

That extra height is useful for anamorphic capture, for framing for different deliverables, and for reframing in post. At launch, there are two readout modes: 9.6K 1.5:1 Open Gate, which uses the full sensor, and 9.6K 2.20:1, with a diagonal of about 59mm, which suits more lenses. Sony says more readout modes will come with future VENICE 2 software updates. In my opinion, the 2.20:1 mode is the one many productions will use first. Many of the large-format lenses announced this year, such as the ZEISS Panoptes 65 primes and the Angénieux EZ 65 zooms, cover an image circle of about 60mm. That fits the 2.20:1 mode, but the full Open Gate needs glass made for true 65mm coverage.

Why the cable matters

The RIALTO name tells you how this works. As with the Rialto Extension System 2 and the VENICE 2 Extension System Mini, the head can move away from the body. In Extension Mode, a cable connects the two. It detaches at both ends, and Sony includes a 4.5m / 14.8ft cable, with a 12m / 39.4ft cable as an option. In Studio Mode, the head attaches directly to the body as one camera.

This is where I think Sony has a strong argument. Until now, digital 65mm meant a big camera. A 1.5kg head on a cable can go on a gimbal, into a car interior, or onto a handheld rig, while the body, media, and power stay somewhere else. The head also records tilt and roll as metadata for post.

Same VENICE 2 pipeline

The VENICE 2 body does the recording. So the RIALTO 65 writes to the same AXS cards, in the same 16-bit X-OCN, with S-Log3 and S-Gamut3 and the CineAlta color science that VENICE users know. For rental houses with VENICE 2 packages, this is the real selling point: the media, accessories, and post workflows stay the same. My feeling is that this is Sony’s main strategy here. It does not need to sell a new camera body, only a new front end for bodies that are already out there. That is my guess, of course.

What we do not know yet is how the sensor performs. Our VENICE 2 Lab Test gives a reference for the full-frame 8.6K version. Rolling shutter on a 9.6K sensor of this size is the first thing I want to see in our lab (Sony, if you are reading this, we are ready when you are).

Lenses, anamorphic, and ND

The RIALTO 65 has no lens mount of its own. Sony designed it for third-party lens mount adapters, so each production selects the mount for its lenses, including 65mm optics. With a lens and adapter that communicate with the camera, it records focal length, focus position, and aperture as metadata for editing, VFX, and virtual production.

This is a change from the Extension System Mini, which ships with E-mount and an ARRI PL adapter. It gives more freedom, but it also adds one more cost and one more decision for the camera team. Sony has not named any adapter makers yet, and I hope to find out more at Pinewood (but we can see a Gecko Cam Adapter on some of the press photos they provided).

For anamorphic work, there is de-squeeze display at multiple ratios and a Zoom to Fit function to check framing. The head also takes 11 drop-in ND filters with electronic contacts, so the VENICE 2 reads the density of each filter automatically. A spare CBK-NDK6510 ND Filter Kit will be available, but Sony says you cannot buy single filters separately.

Price and availability

The RIALTO 65 (CBK-6510XS), the CBK-NDK6510 ND Filter Kit, and the CBK-12C6510 12m cable all arrive in the first half of 2027. Sony has not announced prices, and B&H and CVP do not list the system yet.

For context, the full-frame VENICE 2 Extension System Mini launched at $25,000 at B&H. Sony has not said how the RIALTO 65 will be priced in relation to it. For more information, please visit the Sony website.

Sony now has a 65mm option that plugs into the VENICE 2 system and works on a cable, and I am curious to see it in person today. Would a 1.5:1 sensor change how you frame, or would you mostly use the 2.20:1 mode? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: FUJIFILM Fujikina NYC 2026 Recap – Real Images, Real Community, and No AI Talk
entry.summary: I flew to New York for FUJIFILM’s Fujikina NYC 2026 with no shoot, no interviews and no schedule, just a camera and three days on the Lower East Side. What I found was a photography festival where nobody talked about AI, and where more than three quarters of the visitors were new
entry.content:
I flew to New York for FUJIFILM’s Fujikina NYC 2026 with no shoot, no interviews and no schedule, just a camera and three days on the Lower East Side. What I found was a photography festival where nobody talked about AI, and where more than three quarters of the visitors were new to FUJIFILM, according to the company’s own numbers.

This was a strange trip for me. I travel a lot for CineD, to trade shows, press events and shoots, and that usually means a calendar packed from breakfast to midnight. This time, FUJIFILM invited us to Fujikina NYC 2026, a three-day community festival of photography from October 16 to 18, and my only job was to take it all in. If you read my preview of the program a few weeks ago, you know I went through every bookable session before the trip. On site, I mostly left the plan in my pocket.

A $10 ticket and nine venues

The format is simple. A $10 Experience Pass got you into most of the festival, and some of the workshops and photowalks cost a small extra fee. Everything happened in nine venues spread across a few blocks of the Lower East Side, with the FUJIFILM Brand House at the center.

On my first day, I was told that more than 6,500 people had signed up and that around 70% of them had never been in contact with FUJIFILM before. The final numbers that FUJIFILM sent me after the event are even higher: 7,564 tickets sold, and more than three quarters of the visitors were new to the company. For a brand that has been in the photography business for as long as FUJIFILM, that is remarkable, and in my opinion it is the most important number of the whole weekend.

The FUJIFILM Brand House was the center of Fujikina NYC. Image credit: Nino Leitner (CineD)

Jonas Rask and the photographers behind the program

FUJIFILM hosted dozens of talks, workshops and presentations, with a strong focus on street photography, and according to the company, almost every bookable session was fully booked.

The person who impressed me most was Jonas Rask. He is a Danish street photographer and, in his day job, a medical doctor. He also shoots FUJIFILM’s product images, and has done so since 2019. But what people really know him for is his street photography: double exposures, and a very precise eye for shape and form. Take a look at his portfolio and you will see what I mean. That he does all of this on the side, just for the fun of it, is amazing to me.

Jonas is only one example of the many talented photographers and filmmakers who presented their work and their methods at Fujikina.

Photowalks, and why I took photos again

What I liked most about the format is that the inspiration does not stay in the lecture room. The photowalks take you straight out into the city, often with the same photographer you just listened to. After the first day, I was one of those inspired visitors myself. For the first time in years, I walked the streets of a city with a camera and no plan, no shot list and no client. I simply had fun taking photos again.

Meeting so many people with the same interest in one place gets your creativity going like nothing else.

A street fair, and free camera loans

On Saturday, the festival closed an entire street, Ludlow Street, for a street fair. There were circus performers that you could photograph or film, and a number of tents from photography and filmmaking accessory manufacturers.

But this was not a trade show. Nobody really talked about gear. The conversations were about the photos, about the community, and about having something to say with your images.

Gear was still there, of course, for the people who wanted it. At the Brand House, visitors could borrow FUJIFILM cameras and lenses free of charge and use them during the festival. People loved that. (FUJIFILM, if you are reading this: next time, a corner with the GFX ETERNA 55 and the ETERNA ProRemote app for the video people would be very welcome.)

ICP, World Press Photo and the exhibitions

What makes the event more than pretty pictures and good vibes is the partners. The most important ones were the International Center of Photography (ICP), Magnum Photos, World Press Photo and FotoFest. ICP was itself one of the nine venues, which was very practical.

Some of the exhibitions celebrate FUJIFILM’s own history, such as 15 Years of X Series. Others deal with some of the most urgent social issues of our time, for example Laia Abril’s exhibition at ICP, On Rape and Institutional Failure, and the World Press Photo Exhibition 2026.

During the festival, World Press Photo also announced an extended strategic partnership with FUJIFILM. The point of it is to support photojournalism around the world, and to show reality as it is in an increasingly unstable world. I think that matters a lot right now.

Not a single word about AI

Here is the thing I keep thinking about since I came back. This was 100% an event about real connections and real images. In three days, I did not hear the word AI once. Nobody ignored the topic on purpose. People simply did not care, because nothing beats getting together like this, everyone with their own style and their own perspective on the world, and with a lot of respect for each other and for human creation in particular.

In my opinion, this is very much in line with FUJIFILM’s philosophy, and you could see it in everything they did there. The festival was not about the technology. It was about using that technology to make images that mean something, and about building connections between the people who make them. We recently wrote about how Canon, Nikon, Sony and FUJIFILM see the future of cameras and AI, and in New York I saw one possible answer in practice.

Yes, AI has a huge influence on our jobs, in photography and in filmmaking. I do not want to pretend otherwise. But my feeling is that even average viewers prefer real images, and a festival like this one shows that a lot of people want real images, real connections and real community. In a world that becomes more artificial every day, going back to the roots looks like the way forward to me, and FUJIFILM is celebrating exactly that.

What comes next

FUJIFILM sees the festival as a start. According to the company, it wants to keep building the photography community in New York with local partners such as ICP, and take the same approach to other US cities with Create With Us: On Tour, its regional event series. Photographers Reuben Wu, Casey Cavanaugh and Jonas Rask all told FUJIFILM that Fujikina NYC was the best photography festival ever held in the US. For my part, I came back home more inspired for my own creative work than I have been in a long time, and I can’t wait to get back out there and shoot more.

My advice to FUJIFILM, and honestly to the whole industry: do more events like this. Don’t focus on the tech. Focus on the community, on the connections, and on learning from each other. That has always worked, and it still works in 2026.

A big thank you also goes to my wife, Anita. When I travel like this, the real work waits at home with the kids, and she makes it possible for me to live my passion.

Have you been to a Fujikina event, in New York or in Europe, or would you go to one? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: SmallHD Focus 504 Announced – 5-Inch 1000-Nit Monitor With 3G-SDI, HDMI 2.0, and Wi-Fi Camera Control
entry.summary: SmallHD has brought back the Focus name with the Focus 504, a 5-inch 1080p touchscreen monitor in an aluminum body that weighs 310g. It has 3G-SDI and HDMI 2.0 inputs and outputs, a built-in Sony L-Series battery slot, locking USB-C ports, and internal 2.4GHz Wi-Fi for wireless c
entry.content:
SmallHD has brought back the Focus name with the Focus 504, a 5-inch 1080p touchscreen monitor in an aluminum body that weighs 310g. It has 3G-SDI and HDMI 2.0 inputs and outputs, a built-in Sony L-Series battery slot, locking USB-C ports, and internal 2.4GHz Wi-Fi for wireless camera control. At $999, it becomes the entry point to SmallHD’s current 5-inch range, but it is far from a budget monitor.

SmallHD has added the new Focus 504 to its online store and to a dedicated Focus landing page. The company describes it as its “smallest, slimmest monitor yet”. The 4.97-inch IPS touchscreen has a 1920 x 1080 resolution (443ppi), a maximum brightness of 1000 nits, and a 60Hz refresh rate. The monitor processes video at 10-bit on an 8-bit panel. Video connections are full-size: one 3G-SDI BNC input and output, and one full-size HDMI 2.0 input and output, with cross-conversion in both directions. A locking USB-C “PVC” port carries power, video, and data, and two more locking USB-C ports supply accessory power and take a USB flash drive. The monitor runs PageOS 6, and an internal 2.4GHz Wi-Fi module is ready for wireless camera control of ARRI, Sony, RED, and Canon cameras. SmallHD says that this function is “coming soon” and that licenses are sold separately.

SmallHD aims the Focus 504 at lightweight camera builds, handheld operation, gimbal rigs, and small productions. The name will be familiar to many readers. The original 5-inch SmallHD FOCUS launched at $499 with a 1280 x 720, 800-nit panel and micro HDMI input, and SmallHD later added SDI, OLED, and Focus Pro versions for RED cameras. The Focus 504 keeps the compact idea but moves up in build quality, brightness, and price.

Body, size, and mounting

The Focus 504 uses an anodized aluminum unibody with a raised protective bezel around the screen. SmallHD lists the dimensions as 136 x 88 x 23.9mm / 5.35 x 3.46 x 0.94in and the weight as 0.31kg / 0.68lb without a battery. That is light for a monitor with full-size SDI and HDMI connectors.

There are four 1/4″-20 mounting points (top, bottom, left, and right), and each has ARRI locating pins. Physical controls are a rear joystick, a back button, and two custom function buttons, in addition to the touchscreen. Operating temperature is 0°C to 40°C / 32°F to 105°F.

The display: bright, but not the brightest in the range

At 1000 nits, the Focus 504 is daylight-viewable in most conditions, but it does not match the 2000 nits of the Cine 5 or the 3000 nits of the Ultra 5. Contrast is 1000:1, and the backlight is edge-lit and adjustable.

On color, the SmallHD material is not consistent. The product text says 100% Rec.709 coverage, while the technical spec table on the same page lists 97% Rec.709. Until SmallHD clarifies this, we take 97% as the safer figure. The monitor stores a 33-point calibration LUT internally, and it supports 17-point user LUTs from removable media. A 17-point LUT can also go downstream on the SDI, HDMI, or USB-C output.

Inputs, outputs, and signal support

On SDI, the Focus 504 accepts 3G-SDI, HD-SDI, and SD-SDI signals in YCC 4:2:2 10-bit, up to 1080p60. The HDMI 2.0 input takes signals up to 2160p30 and 1080p120, and the monitor displays them on its 1080p panel. Both SDI and HDMI have loop outputs, and the monitor can cross-convert HDMI to SDI and SDI to HDMI. This is useful when a mirrorless camera with HDMI only must feed an SDI wireless transmitter or a director’s monitor.

Audio comes in through HDMI or SDI, with metering for up to eight channels and a 3.5mm headphone jack for monitoring.

The USB-C setup is the most interesting change. SmallHD calls the main locking port “PVC” (power, video, communication). According to SmallHD, it accepts power input or output, DisplayPort Alt Mode video input, and USB data, depending on the connected device, cable, and firmware. The two other locking USB-C ports give 5V/1.5A accessory power and USB data. Users can plug in a USB-C flash drive to update firmware, load LUTs, and save screen grabs. A 16GB SmallHD USB-A/C flash drive comes in the box, together with a clear screen protector.

Power options

There are three ways to power the Focus 504:

  • a built-in Sony L-Series battery slot
  • a locking 2-pin input that accepts 10V to 17V
  • the locking PVC USB-C port, at 5V to 20V and up to 25W

SmallHD rates power consumption at 10W for the monitor alone and 35W maximum. The company recommends a 12V to 15V DC supply at approximately 2.5A or more.

PageOS 6, vertical mode, and camera control

The Focus 504 runs PageOS 6, which we covered when SmallHD rolled it out to all current monitors. Users build custom pages from tools such as false color (rainbow, ARRI style, or custom with up to 10 nodes), dual zebras, waveform, vectorscope, RGB parade, histogram, focus assist, and peaking. Other tools include frame guides, pixel zoom up to 8x, image flip and rotate, and anamorphic de-squeeze at 0.75x, 1.33x, 1.5x, 1.66x, 2.0x, and 2.5x. Teradek RT overlays are also on the tool list.

The monitor also has the Vertical Mode portrait interface that arrived with the PageOS update that added Fleet Control and Canon camera control. Fleet Control can also load LUTs.

The Wi-Fi module is the feature that separates the Focus 504 from earlier small SmallHD monitors. SmallHD says that it will let the monitor control select RED, ARRI, Canon, and Sony cameras without a control cable. The spec table names ARRI, Sony VENICE, RED DSMC2, and RED RCP2 cameras (KOMODO and DSMC3), while the marketing text adds Canon, for which SmallHD already sells wired camera control for its Cinema EOS cameras. Note that camera control is not active at launch: SmallHD says it is “coming soon”, and each camera license costs extra. The three USB-C ports also support wired camera control protocols.

Accessories

SmallHD sells a Focus 504 Sunhood for $129. It mounts without tools, has magnetic top and side flaps, and has a microfiber interior that protects the screen when folded down. A replacement bottom flag costs $29, and a spare clear screen protector costs $29.99.

Where does it fit?

In SmallHD’s current 5-inch range, the Focus 504 sits below the Cine 5 ($1,649) and the Ultra 5 ($2,249). The main difference is brightness: 1000 nits against 2000 and 3000 nits. Compared with the original Focus, the price has doubled. Many 5-inch monitors from other brands with similar brightness cost much less, and some of them also record. The Focus 504 does not record video. Its value is in PageOS, the SDI and HDMI cross-conversion, the aluminum build, and the camera control function. The launch also comes after a difficult financial period for SmallHD’s parent company Videndum.

Price and availability

The SmallHD Focus 504 costs $999 at B&H, and €914.71 at CVP.

Are 1000 nits and Wi-Fi camera control enough to justify $999 for a 5-inch monitor, or do you prefer a cheaper monitor-recorder for your handheld rig? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Apple Touch Screen MacBook Pro Announced – PROLED XDR Tandem OLED Display, M5 Pro and M5 Max, Genlock
entry.summary: The MacBook Pro many of us have been waiting for is finally here: Apple has announced a new MacBook Pro with a tandem OLED display it calls PROLED XDR, rated at 2000 nits peak, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and more than 80 percent Rec. 2020 coverage. It is also the first Mac wit
entry.content:
The MacBook Pro many of us have been waiting for is finally here: Apple has announced a new MacBook Pro with a tandem OLED display it calls PROLED XDR, rated at 2000 nits peak, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and more than 80 percent Rec. 2020 coverage. It is also the first Mac with a touch screen, it supports genlock, and it is lighter than the current models. Inside are the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that Apple introduced in March. I personally can’t wait to get my hands on one for a review.

Let me get the big picture out of the way first. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display comes in 14-inch and 16-inch versions, with screen diagonals of 14.2 and 16.3 inches. The tandem OLED panel delivers up to 1000 nits sustained full-screen brightness and 2000 nits peak for HDR content, plus up to 2000 nits peak SDR brightness in outdoor conditions. Minimum brightness is 1 nit. The color gamut covers P3 and now also Adobe RGB, and Apple quotes more than 80 percent Rec. 2020 coverage. ProMotion runs from 10Hz to 120Hz, and the fixed refresh rates of 47.95, 48, 50, 59.94 and 60Hz carry over. The M5 Pro version has up to 64GB of unified memory, and the M5 Max version has up to 128GB and up to 16TB of storage. Three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI and an SDXC slot stay, and the 14-inch model now weighs 1.38kg / 3.0lb. Prices start at $2,899.

An OLED MacBook Pro has been rumored for years, and a touch screen Mac for even longer (Apple spent a good part of the last decade explaining why it would never build one). Now both arrive in one machine, and that is why I think this is a bigger deal than the usual chip refresh. We have had touch screens with a keyboard on Windows laptops and on the iPad with a Magic Keyboard for a long time, but neither gives you the full macOS with Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro and every plugin and driver you rely on. To have the benefits of touch combined with a keyboard and the full power of macOS is groundbreaking, and I say that as someone who is usually the first to roll his eyes at Apple’s keynote adjectives.

Where this sits in the lineup

This is not a replacement for the Liquid Retina XDR MacBook Pro. Apple continues to sell the mini-LED models next to the new ones: the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 that we covered yesterday, and the 14-inch and 16-inch models with M5 Pro and M5 Max that Apple announced in March together with the Studio Display XDR. The PROLED XDR models use exactly the same chip configurations as those M5 Pro and M5 Max machines, and in Apple’s US store each PROLED XDR configuration costs $400 more than the Liquid Retina XDR model with the same chip.

So the choice between the two lines is a choice of display, weight and Touch, not of processing power. My guess is that this is a deliberate transition year: Apple gets the OLED panels into the hands of the people who will pay for them first, and the mini-LED models stay as the “value” option until the next chip generation. But that is just my guess.

What the PROLED XDR panel changes

According to Apple, the tandem OLED stack has changes in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the screen and reduce the internal reflections that are common in OLED designs. A display engine controls the color and luminance of each pixel at sub-millisecond intervals. It compensates for content, pixel use, temperature and environment, and it monitors the use of each pixel over time to keep image quality consistent (in plain words: this is Apple’s answer to burn-in, and I want to see how it holds up after a year of timelines with static UI elements). Apple calibrates every panel at the factory for luminance, white point and color gamut.

Compared with the mini-LED Liquid Retina XDR display, the figures move in the direction that matters for HDR review. Peak HDR brightness goes from 1600 to 2000 nits, and the contrast ratio goes from 1,000,000:1 to 10,000,000:1. Because OLED controls light at the pixel level, there is no local-dimming zone structure, so the blooming around bright objects on dark backgrounds that we all know from mini-LED panels should be gone. That alone is worth a lot to anyone who has tried to judge a night exterior on the current MacBook Pro screen. The resolution changes a little: the 14.2-inch panel has 3024 x 1986 pixels and the 16.3-inch panel has 3472 x 2266 pixels, both at 254ppi. The 16-inch screen grows from 16.2 inches because of thinner borders.

The antireflective coating is new, and the optional nano-texture finish is now etched directly into the cover glass. On set, high SDR brightness and lower reflections are more useful than the HDR peak, because the laptop screen is often the only monitor you have for a quick check of the footage.

Reference modes, calibration and genlock

For color work, the reference mode list is the most useful part of the spec sheet. It includes HDR Video (P3-ST 2084), HDTV Video (BT.709-BT.1886), NTSC Video (BT.601 SMPTE-C), PAL and SECAM Video (BT.601 EBU), Digital Cinema (P3-DCI) and Digital Cinema (P3-D65), as well as photography, print, design and sRGB modes. Two new Apple XDR Display presets cover P3 at 2000 nits, and P3 plus Adobe RGB at 2000 nits in one preset. There are also two DICOM medical imaging modes, which Apple limits to nondiagnostic review, research and education.

The Apple Pro Display Calibrator lets you calibrate the panel to specific targets. Apple also says that, through a system it calls Apple Color Matching Function 2026, the display gives a consistent image together with the iPhone 18 Pro and the Studio Display XDR. If that works as advertised, reviewing iPhone footage on the laptop and finishing on the external XDR monitor becomes a lot less of a guessing game. We will test this.

Genlock is the feature with the most direct relevance to production, and the one I did not expect on a laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display can synchronize the refresh rate of a display with the capture of a camera, to reduce ghosting, tearing and other artifacts when the screen is in the shot. Apple names virtual production and on-set work as applications. According to Apple, genlock requires compatible third-party hardware and software, and the press release does not name any (I hope Blackmagic and AJA are reading this). Genlock appears in the tech specs of the PROLED XDR models, but not in those of the Liquid Retina XDR MacBook Pro.

Touch in Final Cut Pro and DaVinci Resolve

The second large change is Touch. The touch sensor is built into the display panel, not added as a separate layer, which Apple says reduces latency. A new hinge design gives the screen more stability when you push on it. macOS 27 translates touches into clicks, so existing apps work at once, and new system gesture APIs let developers build specific touch controls.

In Final Cut Pro, editors can use Touch to mark ranges, drop clips into position and pinch to zoom in on a cut. These changes come with the Apple Creator Studio update in November, which also adds touch controls in Pixelmator Pro and an onscreen polyphonic keyboard with chord and drum pads in Logic Pro. Among third-party apps, Apple lists DaVinci Resolve and Adobe Lightroom for photo and video work, and Blender and Shapr3D for 3D. Apple says these third-party apps will get Touch support later this year, and it does not say what the Resolve implementation will include. I am almost 100% certain Blackmagic will not stop at translating taps into clicks, because the color page with its wheels and curves is an obvious candidate for direct touch, but we will have to wait and see.

The important part for me is that Touch is an addition to the keyboard and trackpad, not a replacement. Nobody will cut a feature film by poking at a vertical screen all day. But marking a range with a finger, zooming into a timeline with a pinch, or nudging a mask point directly on the image while the other hand stays on the keyboard, that is the kind of thing that can make a long edit day a bit faster and a bit less tiring. Whether it does, only hands-on time will tell.

M5 Pro and M5 Max for 8K post

The chip lineup is the same as in the Liquid Retina XDR M5 Pro and M5 Max models, so there are no surprises here. The M5 Pro comes with a 15-core CPU (5 super cores, 10 performance cores) and 16-core GPU, or an 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores) and 20-core GPU, with 307GB/s of memory bandwidth and 24GB, 48GB or 64GB of unified memory. Its Media Engine has one video decode engine, one video encode engine, one ProRes encode and decode engine and AV1 decode. The M5 Max has an 18-core CPU with a 32-core GPU (36GB of memory, 460GB/s) or a 40-core GPU (48GB, 64GB or 128GB, 614GB/s). It doubles the video encode and ProRes engines. Both chips accelerate H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW in hardware and have a Neural Accelerator in each GPU core.

Apple positions the M5 Pro for work such as editing multiple streams of 8K ProRes, and the M5 Max for VFX, 3D animation, film scores and 8K post-production. Storage starts at 1TB on M5 Pro models and 2TB on M5 Max models, and the M5 Max can now be configured with up to 16TB (at Apple’s storage prices, you will want to sit down before you configure that one). According to Apple, a new thermal design keeps the same sustained performance in the lighter chassis and directs warm air away from the display, which makes sense, because heat is the enemy of OLED longevity.

Ports, battery and weight

Connectivity matches the current MacBook Pro: three Thunderbolt 5 ports at up to 120Gb/s, HDMI with multichannel audio output, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe 3 and a 3.5mm headphone jack. The M5 Pro drives up to three external displays and the M5 Max up to four, in addition to the built-in screen. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 come from Apple’s N1 chip, and the 12MP Center Stage camera supports Desk View. The six-speaker system gets new woofers with what Apple says is 50 percent deeper bass, and a new tuning for closed-lid use with an external display.

The 14-inch model weighs 1.38kg / 3.0lb with M5 Pro and 1.40kg / 3.1lb with M5 Max, and it measures 31.08 x 21.63 x 1.50cm / 12.24 x 8.52 x 0.59in. The 16-inch model weighs 1.82kg / 4.0lb (M5 Pro) or 1.84kg / 4.1lb (M5 Max) and measures 35.55 x 24.42 x 1.60cm / 14.0 x 9.62 x 0.63in. Apple says the 14-inch model is half a pound lighter and the 16-inch model 0.7lb lighter than before. Anyone who carries a 16-inch model through airports will appreciate that.

Battery life depends on size and chip. The 16-inch model with a 100Wh battery and M5 Pro reaches the headline 24 hours of video streaming (22 hours with M5 Max). The 14-inch model with a 72.6Wh battery is rated at 22 hours with M5 Pro and 20 hours with M5 Max. Apple’s figures are for 1080p streaming in Safari, so they say nothing about a day of editing or grading at full brightness, which is the number I actually want to know. The 14-inch model fast-charges to 50 percent in 30 minutes with a 96W or higher adapter, and the 16-inch model needs 140W or more.

macOS 27 and software support

The new MacBook Pro ships with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which adds the Dynamic Island to the Mac as a place for Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. As with any new Mac, it will not run older macOS versions. In our look at macOS 27 for video editors, Adobe and Apple had confirmed support, while Avid had not yet qualified Media Composer. If you work with Media Composer, or with plugins and I/O drivers that have no Golden Gate statement yet, check with your vendors before you order. For desktop setups with more media engines, see our Mac Studio M5 Ultra launch coverage.

Price and availability

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display starts at $2,899 with M5 Pro (15-core CPU, 24GB, 1TB) and $4,499 with M5 Max. The 16-inch model starts at $3,399 with M5 Pro and $4,799 with M5 Max. Education prices start at $2,749, $4,199, $3,199 and $4,499. In Germany, Apple lists the four base models at €3,299, €5,199, €3,899 and €5,599 including VAT. Nano-texture glass adds $150 in the US. Pre-orders are open in 30 countries and regions, and deliveries and in-store availability start on November 6. For more information, please visit the Apple website or read Apple’s announcement.

Is a tandem OLED screen with genlock and Touch worth $400 over the mini-LED MacBook Pro for your work, or do you grade on an external monitor anyway? And are you thinking about getting one? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: COMAN T1 Mini One-Touch Tripod Launched on Kickstarter
entry.summary: COMAN just launched the T1 Mini on Kickstarter, a compact carbon fiber travel tripod weighing 1.65kg/3.5 lbs and supporting payloads up to 6kg/13 lbs. It keeps the T1’s one-touch leg system and adds a bolt-style Arca-Swiss quick-release ball head, three leg angles, and a modular
entry.content:
COMAN just launched the T1 Mini on Kickstarter, a compact carbon fiber travel tripod weighing 1.65kg/3.5 lbs and supporting payloads up to 6kg/13 lbs. It keeps the T1’s one-touch leg system and adds a bolt-style Arca-Swiss quick-release ball head, three leg angles, and a modular center column you can invert or swap. So, let’s take a closer look at it!

Founded in 2010, COMAN is a Chinese manufacturer based in Zhongshan that designs and manufactures photo and video support equipment in-house. You might remember the Ulanzi & COMAN Zero Y lightweight travel tripod we talked about at IBC 2022.

The T1 Mini is COMAN’s third crowdfunding campaign, following the COMAN Go! M1 Series one-touch monopod and the COMAN Go! Series T1 tripod. According to the company, T1 users asked for a more compact, travel-friendly version that kept its core features, and the T1 Mini is the answer.

COMAN T1 Mini – specifications

The COMAN T1 Mini weighs 1.65kg/3.5 lbs and can take payloads up to 6kg/13 lbs. It reaches a maximum height of 1,595mm/62.8″, or 2,285mm/89.9″ with the optional PH110 Light Stand Shaft. The folded length is 533mm/20.98″, so the T1 Mini should fit in or on the side of most backpacks.

The T1 Mini features four-section legs, and three preset leg angles allow you to adapt to slopes, stairs, or uneven ground. The tripod also includes interchangeable rubber feet and steel spikes.

It is made of 3K, 10-layer carbon fiber, 6-series aluminum alloy, and stainless steel. The panoramic ball head offers 360° pan and uses a bolt-style Arca-Swiss quick release.

The T1 Mini features two ARRI-style 1/4″-20 threads at the tripod base for attaching accessories such as a monitor, microphone, light, or magic arm.

COMAN T1 Mini – one-touch leg system and center column

Unlocking, extending, and locking each leg section of a traditional tripod takes time. To speed things up, the T1 Mini uses the company’s proprietary one-touch leg system: flip open the clamps, let the leg sections slide out to the desired length, and close the clamps to lock everything in place. COMAN claims a setup time of as little as 3 seconds.

To keep the tripod as compact as possible when folded, COMAN replaced the traditional round center column with a Y-shaped column with a concave-triangular profile. The three legs nest into its grooves when folded, reducing total storage volume by 30%, according to the company.

The center column is also modular and can be configured in several ways:

  • Inverted center shaft: remove the bottom hook, pull out the center shaft, reverse it, and reinstall it for low-angle, ground-level, and macro shots.
  • PH100 Short Center Shaft: included in the box, it replaces the standard center shaft for low-angle shooting. Its 3/8″-16 mounting point also lets you use your favorite photo/video heads.
  • PH110 Light Stand Shaft: sold separately, it extends the tripod height to 2,285mm/89.9″ and turns it into a light stand or 360° camera stand.

COMAN T1 Mini – ball head and quick-release system

The T1 Mini comes with a panoramic ball head that rotates 360° horizontally for panoramas. COMAN says the head uses a US-patented inverted-bowl design that keeps the folded profile compact while still offering a wide tilt range, in both landscape and portrait orientations.

Instead of a traditional knob, the head uses COMAN’s in-house Arca-Swiss quick-release system with a bolt-style side latch. Sliding the latch releases the plate, so you can mount or remove your camera in about one second. The company says the clamp is compatible with 99% of Arca-Swiss plates on the market, including Peak Design-compatible plates.

Last but not least, the optional COMAN DP59 Magnetic Arca-Swiss Mount allows you to attach a smartphone magnetically to the tripod. It can also hold a smartphone next to your camera, for example, to use it as a teleprompter or for live-view monitoring.

Price and availability

The COMAN T1 Mini is now available to preorder on Kickstarter, starting at $279.99 for the Black version and $299.99 for the special-edition Silver and Military Green versions. All three versions share the same specifications.

The tripod ships with a soft carrying pouch, an Arca-Swiss quick-release plate, the PH100 Short Center Shaft, a dedicated adjustment wrench, and a user manual.

For more information, please visit COMAN’s Kickstarter page here.

We are saying this at the end of every crowdfunding-related article: be aware of the risks when backing a project on a crowdfunding platform. Please read the platform’s terms of use, and keep in mind that product delivery can be significantly delayed. Some projects may not be delivered at all. COMAN has a good track record regarding crowdfunding campaigns; their two previous Kickstarter campaigns raised over $216K for the Go! M1 Series and over $174K for the Go! Series T1, and they delivered both to backers on time.

What do you think about the COMAN T1 Mini? Have you already used COMAN tripods before? Do you usually travel with a tripod, and is setup speed important to you? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Accsoon CineView Master 4K II Introduced – DCI 4K60 Transmission, USB-C Output on Both Ends, Camera Control
entry.summary: Accsoon has introduced the CineView Master 4K II, the second generation of its tri-band 4K60 wireless video system. The core transmission platform stays the same, but the receiver now gets its own USB-C video output, and the transmitter adds a dedicated port for camera control fr
entry.content:
Accsoon has introduced the CineView Master 4K II, the second generation of its tri-band 4K60 wireless video system. The core transmission platform stays the same, but the receiver now gets its own USB-C video output, and the transmitter adds a dedicated port for camera control from a phone or tablet. Let’s take a look at what has changed.

The CineView Master 4K II transmits DCI 4K and UHD at up to 60fps with H.265 encoding, and it operates on the 2.4GHz, 5GHz and 6GHz bands at the same time through Accsoon’s proprietary RTMS 4.0 protocol. Accsoon specifies a latency below 25ms at 1080p60 and below 35ms at 4K60 (camera latency excluded), and a range of up to 2.5km (1.55mi). Both the transmitter and the receiver now have a USB-C video output for wired monitoring on a phone or tablet, and up to 10 devices can monitor the feed at the same time. A new USB-C camera-control port on the transmitter lets crews start and stop recording and change exposure settings through the Accsoon SEE app. The transmitter-and-receiver kit costs $899.

We first saw the original CineView Master 4K at IBC 2024 (see our first look), and we later published a full review of the CineView Master 4K. At IBC 2025, a free firmware update added full H.265 encoding up to 4K60 and raised the receiver limit from four to ten, as we reported in our article on Accsoon’s updates to the SEE app, CineView Master 4K and CineView M7 series. Accsoon positions the new model for directors, cinematographers, camera assistants and production crews who need the camera feed, and some camera controls, at different positions on set.

Camera control through the transmitter

The largest functional change is camera control. A supported camera connects to a dedicated USB-C camera-control port on the transmitter, and a phone or tablet running the Accsoon SEE app then controls it. According to Accsoon, the available functions include record start/stop, touch focus, ISO, aperture, white balance, and shutter speed.

Accsoon sees this as a solution for cameras on cranes, car rigs or other positions that are difficult to reach, and for operators who need to change settings without walking back to the camera. There is one restriction: camera control works only when the mobile device connects to the transmitter over Wi-Fi. It is not available through the receiver’s wired USB-C monitoring connection. Which cameras and which functions are supported depends on the model, and Accsoon keeps the current list on its camera control compatibility page.

Camera control is not new in the CineView family. Accsoon added it to the lower-cost line with the CineView SE 4K and to its monitor-receivers with firmware for the CineView M7 Pro. The Master 4K II now brings the function to the top of the range.

The transmission platform carries over

Accsoon describes the 4K60 workflow, the tri-band transmission and the RTMS 4.0 protocol as the base that the second generation keeps from the first. On paper, the transmission figures are the same as those of the original model. DCI 4K and UHD are supported up to 60fps, and H.265 encoding keeps the bitrate down.

The latency and range figures come with conditions. According to Accsoon, the sub-25ms and sub-35ms latency values were measured with 1080p60 and 4K60 video respectively, both at low bitrates and without camera latency. The 2.5km range was measured with 1080p60 video at a low bitrate, in FCC-compliant operation, in an unobstructed environment with no interference. On a real set, with walls, people and other radio traffic, the range will be shorter.

The press text does not list the video connections of the new model. The first-generation CineView Master 4K has HDMI and 3G-SDI inputs on the transmitter, with 4K only over HDMI and SDI limited to 1080p. Early UK retailer listings for the II show the same layout.

USB-C monitoring at both ends

On the original CineView Master 4K, only the transmitter had a USB-C video output for wired monitoring on a mobile device. The CineView Master 4K II adds a USB-C video output to the receiver too. A crew can now connect a compatible phone or tablet at the camera and at the receiving station, without a separate wireless link for each device.

A typical setup could be an operator with a phone as a camera-side display, and a director or client at the receiver with a tablet on a USB-C cable. Accsoon says that compatible mobile devices also charge while connected, which helps on long shooting days.

Up to 10 devices can monitor the feed at the same time. Accsoon leaves the mix to the production: dedicated receivers at fixed monitoring stations, mobile devices for crew who move around the location, or a combination of both.

Ecosystem, Frame.io and power

The CineView Master 4K II supports Frame.io Camera to Cloud through a compatible mobile workflow. Accsoon lists compatibility with the CineView Master 4K, CineView Master 4K Lite, CineView SE 4K, CineView M7 Pro and CineView M7H Pro. Owners of first-generation receivers or Accsoon monitor-receivers can thus integrate the new transmitter into their current setup. Our article on the CineView M7 series updates has more information on the monitor side.

The transmitter weighs approximately 322g (11.4oz) and the receiver approximately 320g (11.3oz), both without antennas. Power comes from NP-F batteries or an external DC input from 7.4V to 16.8V. Accsoon also offers optional V-Mount and Gold-Mount battery adapters, which are sold separately. We covered the earlier Accsoon V-Lock adapter for the CineView Master 4K when it came out.

Current limitations

Camera control is available only over the Wi-Fi connection to the transmitter, so the wired receiver-side connection cannot be used to change camera settings. The list of supported cameras and functions is set by Accsoon and depends on the camera model. All latency and range values are manufacturer figures measured at low bitrates under ideal conditions. Battery adapters for V-Mount and Gold-Mount are extra.

Price and availability

The Accsoon CineView Master 4K II transmitter-and-receiver kit costs $899. For comparison, the first-generation kit launched at $849. Accsoon has not announced an availability date or EUR pricing in the press text. At the time of writing, we did not find the CineView Master 4K II at B&H, and the CVP listings were not available to link to. For more information, please visit the Accsoon website.

entry.title: Sony LYTIA 720 Announced – 50MP 1/1.56-Inch Mobile Sensor, 4K 60p HDR, 100 dB Dynamic Range
entry.summary: Sony Semiconductor Solutions has announced the LYTIA 720, a 50-megapixel image sensor for the main camera of smartphones. It is not a flagship chip, but it brings technology from Sony’s high-end LYTIA sensors down to the 1/1.56-type format that many mid-range and upper mid-range
entry.content:
Sony Semiconductor Solutions has announced the LYTIA 720, a 50-megapixel image sensor for the main camera of smartphones. It is not a flagship chip, but it brings technology from Sony’s high-end LYTIA sensors down to the 1/1.56-type format that many mid-range and upper mid-range phones use. For mobile video shooters, the interesting part is that the sensor can record 4K at 60fps in HDR with all-pixel autofocus active.

The Sony LYTIA 720 is a stacked CMOS sensor with a 10.24mm diagonal, approximately 50 effective megapixels and 1.0μm pixels behind a Quad Bayer Coding color filter. Sony claims that a new Ultra High Conversion Gain (UHCG) circuit reduces random noise in dark scenes by approximately 50% compared to the LYTIA 700, the previous 1/1.56-type, 50MP sensor in the range. With Hybrid Frame-HDR, Sony quotes a dynamic range of 100 dB. In video, the sensor reads out 4K (16:9) at up to 120fps, or at 60fps with DCG-HDR enabled, and all-pixel autofocus stays active in all listed modes. Sony plans to start mass-production shipments in early November 2026.

We have reported on several LYTIA sensors over the past year. The LYTIA 901 is a 200MP chip designed for lossless in-sensor zoom, and the LYTIA L910 introduced a LOFIC structure for 100 dB from a single exposure. More recently, the telephoto camera of the Vivo X500 Pro debuted the 1/2-type LYTIA 610. The LYTIA 720 sits in a different place: it is a smaller, more mainstream sensor that inherits parts of that technology.

Less noise in low light

The main claim is the low-light performance. UHCG circuit technology increases the efficiency of the charge-to-voltage conversion, which Sony says suppresses the grain that comes from noise in dark environments. The company’s comparison image shows the LYTIA 700 and the LYTIA 720 side by side at 2 lux. Sony describes the result as a brighter image from the new sensor at a similar noise level, rather than a cleaner image at the same brightness.

Sony calls this “industry-leading” low-light performance among mobile CMOS sensors, based on its own research at the time of the announcement. The 50% figure is a comparison with Sony’s own previous product, not a measured result from a third party. For context, the L910 used the same UHCG approach and Sony claimed a 30% noise reduction there, against the larger LYTIA 828.

4K 60p HDR with all-pixel autofocus

For video, the more practical change is in the readout. Sony says it optimized the analog-to-digital (AD) conversion circuits, which reduces the conversion time and also lowers the power consumption of the sensor. According to Sony, the LYTIA 720 is the first 1/1.56-type LYTIA sensor with 1.0μm pixels that records 4K 60fps HDR video with all-pixel autofocus.

The HDR video mode uses single-frame Dual Conversion Gain HDR (DCG-HDR). The sensor reads the same exposure at two conversion gains, so it does not need to merge separate frames that are captured at different times. Sony says this suppresses motion artifacts and keeps a sufficient exposure time for low-noise images. For anyone who has seen ghosting on moving subjects in a phone’s HDR video mode, this is the relevant point.

The frame rates with all-pixel autofocus are as follows. The full 50MP (4:3) readout runs at 30fps. In 12.5MP (4:3) mode, the sensor reaches 90fps, or 30fps with DCG-HDR. 4K2K (16:9) runs at 120fps, or 60fps with DCG-HDR. So 4K 120fps is possible, but only without HDR.

What about the 100 dB figure?

The 100 dB dynamic range comes from Hybrid Frame-HDR (HF-HDR). This technology combines DCG-HDR data, which covers the low to medium brightness range from one exposure, with a separate short-exposure frame for the highlights. The two are merged in post-processing. A dynamic range of 100 dB converts to approximately 16.6 stops.

Two points are important here. First, HF-HDR is not a single-exposure method like the LOFIC-based approach in the L910, because it adds a second, shorter frame for the highlights. Second, the specification table lists only DCG-HDR for the 4K 60fps mode, and Sony does not say at which frame rates HF-HDR is available. The 100 dB figure therefore describes the capability of the sensor with HF-HDR, not necessarily what a phone records in 4K 60p HDR.

Dynamic range figures on a sensor data sheet are also not the same as what reaches the final file. The image processor, noise reduction, tone mapping and codec of each phone all have an effect. Our Lab Tests of various cameras and smartphones show how measured results from finished devices can differ from manufacturer claims.

Interface and power

The sensor uses an analog supply of 2.8V and 1.8V, a digital supply of 1.1V and an interface voltage of 1.8V or 1.2V. Output is via MIPI C-PHY (2 or 3 trios, maximum 4.5 Gsps per trio) or MIPI D-PHY (2 or 4 lanes, maximum 2.5 Gbps per lane). These figures are relevant to phone makers more than to users, but the lower power consumption from the faster AD conversion can have an effect on heat and battery life during long 4K recordings.

Which phones will use it?

Sony does not name any customers in the announcement. The company says only that the 1/1.56-type size is “widely adopted in the smartphone market” and that it wants to bring high-quality imaging to more users. With mass production starting in early November 2026, the first phones with the LYTIA 720 are likely to come from manufacturers that announce them in their own launch events. Until then, there is no confirmed device.

More information about the LYTIA range is on Sony’s LYTIA brand site.

Is a cleaner 4K 60p HDR mode on a mid-size sensor more important to you than larger sensors and higher resolution in phones? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Feiyu Pocket 4 Announced – 1/1.55-Inch Sensor, 4K60, 111GB Built-In Storage
entry.summary: FeiyuTech has launched the Feiyu Pocket 4, its new three-axis gimbal camera and the first update to the line since the Pocket 3. The camera gets a much larger sensor than its predecessor, a 2.64-inch touchscreen that slides down to start shooting and up to cover the lens, and 111
entry.content:
FeiyuTech has launched the Feiyu Pocket 4, its new three-axis gimbal camera and the first update to the line since the Pocket 3. The camera gets a much larger sensor than its predecessor, a 2.64-inch touchscreen that slides down to start shooting and up to cover the lens, and 111GB of internal storage. At $299, it costs a lot less than DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4, but the spec sheet also shows where the money was saved.

The Feiyu Pocket 4 uses a 1/1.55-inch CMOS sensor with 50 megapixels behind a fixed-focus 110° lens at f/2.2. It records UHD 4K up to 60fps, 2.7K up to 60fps, and 1080p up to 120fps as H.264 or HEVC in an MP4 container, with a maximum bitrate of 80 Mbps. Stills go up to 8192 x 6144 pixels. A three-axis mechanical gimbal with up to 450° of pan travel stabilizes the image, and AI face and subject tracking work together with gesture control. The camera has 128GB of eMMC storage (about 111GB available to the user) and no microSD slot, and it weighs about 205g / 7.2oz. FeiyuTech sells the camera directly for $299, or $379 in a Creator Kit.

We last covered FeiyuTech’s pocket cameras when the company introduced the Pocket 2 and Pocket 2S in 2021. Since then, this category has changed a lot. DJI released the Osmo Pocket 4 in April and the dual-lens Osmo Pocket 4P in July, and pocket gimbal cameras are now a major part of the market. Our analysis of how DJI and Insta360 now ship more cameras than the mirrorless industry gives the context. The Pocket 4 is FeiyuTech’s attempt to compete in this segment on price.

A sliding screen in place of a lens cap

The most unusual part of the Pocket 4 is its mechanical design. The 2.64-inch touchscreen (480 x 480 pixels) sits on a sliding frame. Slide it down, and the camera powers on and is ready to shoot. According to FeiyuTech’s launch blog post, magnetic sensing detects the movement. Slide it up one step, and the gimbal motors lock. A second step extends a wraparound cover that encloses the camera head, so no separate case or clamp is necessary for transport.

The square screen is also how FeiyuTech handles framing. The camera natively shoots 4:3, and the user can select 16:9 or vertical 9:16 on the touchscreen without physically turning the camera. According to the manual, vertical video goes up to 3K. The user can also rotate the camera 90° to enter the vertical mode. The body is made of aluminum-magnesium alloy and plastic, and it measures 140.5 x 52 x 31.7mm / 5.53 x 2.05 x 1.25in when folded. The Pocket 4 is not waterproof.

Sensor, lens and recording formats

On paper, the 1/1.55-inch sensor is a large improvement over the Feiyu Pocket 3, which has a 1/2.3-inch, 12-megapixel sensor. It is still smaller than the 1-inch sensor in DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4. The 110° lens is wide for a vlogging camera, and the specifications list it as fixed focus. FeiyuTech’s FAQ states plainly that the Pocket 4 does not support autofocus. Thus, close-up product shots or face-to-camera recording at arm’s length can depend on the depth of field of the small sensor, not on a focus system.

Video options include 4K at 24, 25, 30, 48, 50, and 60fps, 2.7K (2720 x 1520) at the same frame rates, and 1080p at up to 120fps. A separate slow-motion mode records at 2x or 4x in HD or Full HD. Time-lapse (static, dynamic, and motion), panorama, and a night mode are also available. ISO goes from 100 to 3200, and the electronic shutter goes from 16 seconds to 1/8000s. Users can switch between auto and manual exposure, select average or spot metering, and set flicker reduction to 50Hz or 60Hz.

FeiyuTech does not list a log profile, a 10-bit mode, or an HDR mode on the product page or in the manual. The camera menu has a color option, but the company does not say what it includes. Photos are saved as JPG, and the product page also lists JPG+DNG. The maximum video bitrate of 80 Mbps is less than half of the 180 Mbps that DJI specifies for the Osmo Pocket 4.

Tracking, gestures and gimbal control

The mechanical ranges of the three-axis gimbal are −100° to +350° on pan, −185° to +134.5° on tilt, and −90° to +229.5° on roll, with a maximum controllable speed of 180° per second. The follow modes are: all follow, pan and tilt follow, and pan follow, and users can set the pan speed to slow, default, or quick. A five-way joystick controls the pan and tilt axes, and a double-tap switches it to digital zoom.

Face tracking and subject tracking run on the camera itself; the user taps the subject on the touchscreen to select it. On the Pocket 3, tracking required the Feiyu Cam app. Gesture control has four commands: an OK sign starts or stops tracking, an open palm takes a photo or starts recording, a double L shape sets a custom composition, and a double thumbs-up switches gesture control off. The Feiyu Cam app (iOS 13 or later, Android 6.0 or later) connects over 5GHz Wi-Fi and gives remote control, live preview, file transfer, and gimbal control through the phone’s motion sensors.

Storage, battery and connectivity

The 111GB of user storage replaces the memory card completely. FeiyuTech says this holds approximately 875 minutes of Full HD video. At the maximum bitrate of 80 Mbps, the same storage holds roughly three hours of 4K footage. Users who shoot a full day of 4K must offload during the day. Files transfer over USB-C to a computer, directly to some phones over USB-C, or over Wi-Fi to the app. The Pocket 4 also works as a UVC webcam over USB-C.

Power comes from an internal 1300mAh, 7.4V lithium-ion battery. FeiyuTech gives recording times of up to 2.5 hours at 1080p30, 1.8 hours at 4K30, and 1.5 hours at 4K60, measured at 25°C. Audio comes from the built-in microphone as 48kHz AAC. In FeiyuTech’s comparison table, it lists an external microphone as not supported for the Pocket 4, while the Pocket 3 supports one with a dedicated adapter. The Creator Kit includes a “Microphone & Battery Handle”, but FeiyuTech has not yet published specifications for this accessory. The camera also has a 1/4-inch thread on the base.

How it compares with the DJI Osmo Pocket 4

The DJI Osmo Pocket 4 has a 1-inch sensor, 4K at up to 240fps, 10-bit D-Log (a later firmware update extended it to slow motion), autofocus, 107GB internal storage plus a microSD slot, direct DJI Mic pairing, and timecode. It weighs 190.5g. In Europe, it started at €479 at launch. The Feiyu Pocket 4 is heavier and has no log profile, autofocus, external audio input, or card slot. Its advantages are the larger screen, the integrated lens cover, the larger internal storage, and the lower price.

For readers who use a pocket gimbal camera as a B-camera in a professional production, the missing log profile and fixed focus are the main limitations. For travel and vlogging users who shoot mostly 8-bit footage for social media, the Feiyu Pocket 4 is a less expensive choice.

Price and availability

The Feiyu Pocket 4 is available now from the FeiyuTech online store. The Standard Kit costs $299 and includes the camera, a carrying bag, a USB-C to USB-C cable, a USB-A to USB-C adapter, a wrist strap, and the manual. The Creator Kit costs $379 and adds the Microphone & Battery Handle and a tripod. A portable bag ($49) and an adjustable extension pole ($39) are available separately. FeiyuTech ships from local warehouses in the US, Canada, the UK, and Germany, with free shipping to these regions. At the time of writing, B&H does not list the Pocket 4, and FeiyuTech has not published a euro price.

Is the Feiyu Pocket 4’s sliding cover and large internal storage enough to choose it over a DJI Osmo Pocket 4, or are log recording and autofocus necessary for you? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Hollyland LARK M3 Explained – One Transmitter, Up to Four Receivers, and 4-Track Audio
entry.summary: Most budget wireless kits are built around one assumption: one receiver, one camera. The Hollyland LARK M3 breaks that assumption, because a single transmitter can feed up to four receivers at the same time. On a multi-camera interview, that means every camera can record the same
entry.content:
Most budget wireless kits are built around one assumption: one receiver, one camera. The Hollyland LARK M3 breaks that assumption, because a single transmitter can feed up to four receivers at the same time. On a multi-camera interview, that means every camera can record the same clean lav signal instead of scratch audio. Here is how the system divides control between receivers, where the four isolated tracks actually arrive, and where its limits are.

We have previously covered the LARK M2 and the more discreet LARK M2S, as well as the LARK MAX 2, which adds onboard recording and timecode. The M3 sits between those approaches. It keeps the 9g (0.32oz) transmitter size of the M2 while adding 32-bit float output and much more flexible multi-transmitter and multi-receiver routing.

The LARK M3 is a 2.4GHz system with a 9g (0.32oz) transmitter, 48kHz audio at 24-bit or 32-bit float, three levels of AI noise cancellation, and a rated range of up to 300m (1,000ft). It scales in both directions: one receiver accepts up to four transmitters, and one transmitter pairs with up to four receivers, in any combination up to 4TX and 4RX. Two receiver types are available: a 5.9g (0.21oz) USB-C receiver for phones, tablets, and computers, and a 20g (0.71oz) camera receiver with 3.5mm TRS output and a USB-C port.

One lav, several cameras

On a typical two-camera interview with a single wireless kit, the receiver goes on the A camera. The B camera records its onboard microphone as a reference, and the editor syncs the angles by waveform and uses the A-camera audio for the whole scene.

The LARK M3 removes that step. A second, third, or fourth receiver pairs to the same transmitter, so each camera records the lav signal directly. The same applies to mixed setups, which Hollyland confirms in its FAQ: camera receivers and USB-C receivers can work together in one system as long as the total is four receivers or fewer. A presenter can feed a cinema camera, a phone recording a vertical version, and a laptop running a live stream from one transmitter. Transmitters and receivers can also be added or removed during a shoot without interrupting audio on the units that stay connected.

Hollyland has followed a similar logic on the video side. The Pyro Ultra wireless video system supports an unlimited number of receivers, and the LARK M3 brings a smaller version of that one-to-many idea to entry-level audio.

How the primary and secondary receivers divide control

When more than one receiver is connected, the system assigns roles automatically. According to the manual, the first receiver that connects after the transmitter powers on becomes the primary receiver, and every receiver after it becomes a secondary. The primary receiver controls the transmitters: noise cancellation, mute, the indicator lights, voice tuning presets, and Smart Reverb.

Two settings stay independent on every receiver: output gain and channel mode. Each camera can therefore run its own level and channel configuration without changing the transmitter settings for the rest of the system.

If the primary receiver goes offline during a take, the system selects one of the remaining receivers as the new primary while audio on the secondary receivers continues.

The roles can be changed. In the app, a secondary receiver can be promoted to primary, or the crew can disconnect all receivers except the one that should take control, and then reconnect the others.

Where the four isolated tracks actually arrive

The headline feature of four independent tracks needs precise reading, because it depends on the connection.

According to Hollyland’s manual and FAQ, the LARK M3 can record up to four isolated tracks, but only through compatible digital connections. The camera receiver’s 3.5mm TRS output is limited to Mono or Stereo, so four separate tracks require the separately sold LARK M3 Hot Shoe Adapter or a USB-C connection to a computer with compatible recording software.

On phones, 4-Track mode depends on the app. Hollyland’s FAQ says compatible third-party recording apps on iOS can support it, while the native camera apps on iOS and Android do not. The same applies to 32-bit float: it requires compatible software, and Android devices are limited to 24-bit.

Practical configurations

The flexible transmitter and receiver arrangement is what makes the M3 different from a conventional two-person wireless kit.

For a two-person interview on two cameras, both cameras can receive the same two microphones directly. For a four-person panel, four transmitters can feed one receiver, with four isolated tracks available through a compatible digital connection. A single presenter can instead feed several receivers at once, allowing the same microphone to reach a camera, phone and computer simultaneously.

The system can therefore be built around either the number of people being recorded or the number of devices that need to receive the audio.

Current limitations

The LARK M3 transmitters do not have internal recording, and the system does not support timecode. A triple press of the transmitter button starts and stops recording on the connected device, not in the microphone. If the 2.4GHz link drops, no backup copy exists on the transmitter.

Multiple receivers reduce some of that risk because each camera or device holds its own received copy of the audio, but all copies still depend on the same wireless transmission.

Battery life is approximately eight hours per transmitter with noise cancellation off, and 4 to 4.5 hours with it on. The camera receiver runs for approximately nine hours, and receivers can run continuously on USB-C power. Hollyland rates the 300m (1,000ft) range for open environments without interference.

How it compares within the LARK lineup

The LARK M3 keeps the compact 9g (0.32oz) transmitter format of the LARK M2 while adding 32-bit float output, AI noise cancellation, support for up to four transmitters and four receivers, and four-track recording through compatible digital connections.

The LARK MAX 2 moves further toward professional production. Its transmitters add onboard 32-bit float recording and timecode, giving crews a backup copy and a more complete sync workflow.

The M3 therefore makes the most sense when the priority is a small microphone and flexible routing between several people, cameras, or recording devices. The MAX 2 remains the stronger option when internal backup recording and timecode are more important.

Price and availability

The LARK M3 is available now in four kits. The 2TX&1RX kit is priced at $99, the 2TX&2RX kit is $119, the 2TX&4RX kit is $179, and the 4TX&2RX kit costs $179. B&H also sells single components: a transmitter at $39, a USB-C receiver at $29, and a camera receiver at $39. The hot shoe adapter is sold separately. For more information, please visit the Hollyland website.

Would one transmitter feeding several cameras change how you rig your next interview, or is backup recording a requirement before a kit goes on a multi-camera shoot? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 and iMac M6 Announced – 2nm Chip, ProRes RAW Media Engine, Up to 32GB Memory
entry.summary: Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac. Both machines get two more CPU and GPU cores than before, Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, Wi-Fi 7 and a Media Engine with hardware ProRes and ProRes RAW support. For editors, the more import
entry.content:
Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac. Both machines get two more CPU and GPU cores than before, Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, Wi-Fi 7 and a Media Engine with hardware ProRes and ProRes RAW support. For editors, the more important details sit further down the spec sheet: memory stops at 32GB, and the ports stay at Thunderbolt 4.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 and the iMac with M6 at $1,499. Pre-orders open tomorrow, October 28, and deliveries start on Friday, November 6. Both use the M6 chip that debuted in the Mac mini in August, which we covered in our Mac Studio and Mac mini launch article. In its full version, the M6 has a 12-core CPU (2 super cores, 4 performance cores and 6 efficiency cores), a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core, third-generation ray tracing, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine and up to 170GB/s of memory bandwidth. Unified memory starts at 16GB and goes up to 32GB. The Media Engine has one video decode engine, one video encode engine, one ProRes encode and decode engine and AV1 decode, with hardware acceleration for H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW. The entry-level iMac uses a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU version of the chip.

The M6 chip and video work

Apple’s performance claims for the MacBook Pro compare it with the 14-inch M5 model: up to 30 percent faster graphics, up to 25 percent faster AI workloads such as LLM prompt processing, and a Neural Engine that is up to 1.9x faster. The application examples in the press release are Blender ray tracing (up to 1.3x faster than M5), Affinity image processing (up to 1.2x) and Xcode builds (up to 1.3x). For the iMac, Apple compares against the M4 generation and quotes up to 2x faster graphics and up to 5x faster on-device AI prompt processing in LM Studio. Apple also claims the M6 has the world’s fastest CPU core. None of the figures Apple published for these two machines involves a video editing or grading application, so for filmmakers the Media Engine and memory configuration say more than the percentages.

The Media Engine layout is the same as in the M5 Pro: one encoder, one decoder and one ProRes engine. The M5 Max doubles the encode and ProRes blocks. In practice, the M6 machines get hardware decoding for the formats most cameras record (H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW), but parallel exports, for example deliverables and proxies at the same time, share a single encoder. Formats outside that list, such as BRAW, R3D or ARRIRAW, rely on the CPU and GPU instead.

Memory is the more obvious ceiling. Both machines top out at 32GB, and on the MacBook Pro the 16GB base configuration runs at 153GB/s; the full 170GB/s needs 24GB or 32GB. For 4K timelines in Final Cut Pro, Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, 32GB is workable. Heavy noise reduction, Fusion compositions or 8K material are where the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro (up to 64GB at 307GB/s) or M5 Max becomes the more realistic option. We covered those models in our MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max launch article.

MacBook Pro M6: XDR display, Thunderbolt 4

The 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display carries over: 3024 x 1964 pixels at 254ppi, up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 1,600 nits peak for HDR content, a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio, P3 wide color and ProMotion up to 120Hz. For editors, the fixed refresh rates of 47.95, 48, 50, 59.94 and 60Hz match playback to the project frame rate, and the reference modes include HDR Video (P3-ST 2084). A nano-texture version of the display is optional.

On the ports side, the M6 model has three Thunderbolt 4 ports at up to 40Gb/s, plus HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe 3 and a headphone jack. The M5 Pro and M5 Max models have three Thunderbolt 5 ports at up to 120Gb/s instead. The M6 drives up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or one display at 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 are new.

Apple rates the 72.4Wh battery at up to 24 hours of video streaming and up to 16 hours of wireless web use, and says performance is the same on battery and on mains power. The laptop ships with a 70W USB-C adapter; with a 96W or higher adapter, it charges to 50 percent in 30 minutes. It measures 31.26 x 22.12 x 1.55cm / 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61in and weighs 1.55kg / 3.4lb. Storage options are 1TB, 2TB or 4TB, and the colors are space black and silver.

iMac M6: two models, two different port layouts

The iMac comes in two versions, and the differences matter more for media work than the two extra cores suggest. The 10-core model has two Thunderbolt/USB 4 ports, supports one external display (up to 6K/60Hz), takes up to 24GB of memory and up to 1TB of storage, and has 2.5Gb Ethernet only as an option. The 12-core model has four Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, up to 32GB of memory, up to 2TB of storage, support for two external 6K displays (or one 8K/60Hz display) and an optional nano-texture glass. Both start with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD, which Apple says is up to 2x faster than in the M4 iMac. With 256GB, media has to live on external storage from day one.

The 24-inch (23.5-inch viewable) 4.5K Retina display has a resolution of 4480 x 2520 pixels at 218ppi, 500 nits of brightness and P3 wide color with support for 1 billion colors. It has no XDR or HDR mode and no ProMotion, so the iMac is an SDR editing screen. The iMac also has a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six-speaker system with Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support, and a three-mic array. It comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver, measures 54.7 x 46.1cm / 21.5 x 18.1in and weighs 4.42kg / 9.7lb (10-core) or 4.44kg / 9.8lb (12-core).

Both ship with macOS 27

Both computers ship with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which includes Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features. For edit systems, the more relevant point is software support. In our macOS 27 article for video editors, Adobe and Apple had confirmed support, while Blackmagic Design and Avid had not listed macOS 27 as qualified. New Macs generally cannot run a macOS version older than the one they ship with, so anyone buying one of these machines for client work should check their NLE, plugins and I/O drivers first.

Where they fit

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is the entry point to Apple’s pro laptop line. It suits editors and shooters who cut 4K H.264, HEVC or ProRes, offload cards on location with the SDXC slot, and want an XDR display for HDR review away from the suite. Projects that need more than 32GB of memory, fast Thunderbolt 5 RAIDs or three external displays point to the M5 Pro version.

The iMac is an all-in-one for SDR work: proxy editing, assistant editor stations, social and YouTube production, and offices that need a clean setup. For that work, the 12-core model is the better fit, as it adds the two extra Thunderbolt ports, the second external display and Ethernet as standard.

Price and availability

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 ($1,899 for education) with 16GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. In Germany, Apple lists it from €2,299 including VAT. The iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 for the 10-core model and $1,699 for the 12-core model ($1,449 and $1,599 for education), and at €1,799 and €1,999 including VAT in Germany. Pre-orders open on October 28 in 35 countries and regions, and deliveries and in-store availability start on November 6. B&H and CVP do not list the new models yet. More details are in Apple’s announcements for the MacBook Pro and the iMac, and on the MacBook Pro and iMac tech specs pages.

Would an M6 MacBook Pro or iMac cover your editing work, or do 32GB and Thunderbolt 4 push you to the M5 Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Apple Creator Studio Update Announced – MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro, Generate Fill, Cinematic Mode Encoding
entry.summary: Apple has announced what it calls its most exciting update to Apple Creator Studio since the subscription bundle launched in January. Final Cut Pro for Mac now ships with MotionVFX effects and plugins built in, the Content Hub adds stock video, and images move between Final Cut P
entry.content:
Apple has announced what it calls its most exciting update to Apple Creator Studio since the subscription bundle launched in January. Final Cut Pro for Mac now ships with MotionVFX effects and plugins built in, the Content Hub adds stock video, and images move between Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro without reimporting. Let’s take a look at what changes for editors, motion designers and anyone handling sound in post.

The update arrives on the App Store in November as a free update for existing subscribers. In Final Cut Pro for Mac, MotionVFX templates, titles, transitions and graphics sit directly inside the app, together with tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. The Content Hub, Apple’s library of curated stock assets, now includes video and is available inside Final Cut Pro. Editors can send any still image from the timeline to Pixelmator Pro and have the edited version update in the project automatically, and Pixelmator Pro adds Generate Fill for prompt-based image edits.

Final Cut Pro also gets more keyframe easing options, clips that can be disconnected from the primary storyline, and 23 new transcription languages. Motion adds MotionVFX plugins for color grading, 3D camera tracking and one-click selection, plus a new Displacement filter. Compressor can now encode Cinematic mode video from the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Logic Pro gets a redesigned Browser, a Stem Splitter that separates drums, and an intelligent assistant in beta. A subscription costs $12.99 / €12.99 per month or $129 / €129 per year.

We covered the launch of Apple Creator Studio in January, when Apple first bundled Final Cut Pro, Motion, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage and Pixelmator Pro into one subscription. In March, Apple acquired MotionVFX, the Polish developer best known for its Final Cut Pro plugins and templates, and this update is the first time that content appears inside Apple’s own apps. It also follows Final Cut Camera 2.4 and Final Cut Pro 12.4 in September, which added aperture control for the iPhone 18 Pro and Cinematic mode refocusing in post.

MotionVFX content inside Final Cut Pro

According to Apple, Final Cut Pro for Mac now gives editors access to “thousands of elements” from MotionVFX. These include themed templates, graphics, titles and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. Until now, MotionVFX products were separate purchases from the developer’s own store. Apple does not list which individual MotionVFX plugins are included, and the press release does not say whether the one-time-purchase version of Final Cut Pro also receives this content.

The Content Hub is now available inside Final Cut Pro as well. It holds Apple-curated stock video, photos and backgrounds that editors can drop into a timeline to fill gaps or build quick mockups. Apple does not give the size of the video library or the license terms in the press release, so anyone planning to use these clips in client work should check the usage conditions first.

Final Cut Pro also adds generative image creation from text descriptions inside a project, with quick edits and style adjustments. Apple does not name the model behind it.

Workflow changes in the timeline

Apart from the new content, three changes concern day-to-day editing. Keyframe easing gets more options for finer control over animation curves.
